names.value: Egypt — Khedivate under European financial intervention

governments.value: Khedive and cabinet, with European financial controls

existence.note: Bounds delimit accepted researched coverage, not full political lifetime.

governments.value: British high commissioner and Egyptian sultanate

descriptions.value: British protection replaced the prior Ottoman relationship. Nationalist resistance and the 1919 uprising challenged authority; a protectorate does not mean ordinary British sovereign annexation.

existence.note: Bounds delimit accepted researched coverage, not full political lifetime.

names.value: Egypt — kingdom under strengthened royal authority

governments.value: King and cabinet under the strengthened 1930 constitutional arrangement

existence.note: Bounds delimit accepted researched coverage, not full political lifetime.

governments.value: King and cabinet; Parliament within the constitutional framework

existence.note: Bounds delimit accepted researched coverage, not full political lifetime.

existence.note: Bounds delimit accepted researched coverage, not full political lifetime.

politicalStatus.value: Egyptian region within the unitary Egyptian–Syrian republic

governments.value: President Gamal Abdel Nasser

existence.note: Bounds delimit accepted researched coverage, not full political lifetime.

governments.value: Bey and French Resident General

descriptions.value: The narrow postwar framework avoids carrying a named Bey across wartime deposition or treating Axis occupation as uninterrupted ordinary French administration.

existence.note: Bounds delimit accepted researched coverage, not full political lifetime.

names.value: Republic of Tunisia — original 1959 constitutional framework

governments.value: President and unicameral National Assembly

descriptions.value: Original French Articles 18 and 37–43 establish the Assembly and presidential executive choosing responsible ministers. This formal structure is not proof of unrestricted democracy; later amended offices are excluded.

governments.value: French administration; rival GPRA government in exile

politicalStatus.value: Italian colonial framework with negotiated Sanusi autonomy

governments.value: Italian provincial colonial administration; Idris in interior Cyrenaica

descriptions.value: The accord occurred sometime in 1920 without a precise date in the accepted source; conservative coverage starts 1 January 1921 and ends before the 1922 Tripolitanian title dispute. existence.note: Bounds delimit accepted researched coverage, not full political lifetime.

descriptions.value: Occupation government exercised administrative, legislative and judicial functions; this is not British sovereign annexation or the later independent kingdom.

governments.value: British Civil Affairs officers under a brigadier

descriptions.value: A separate Tripoli command retained parts of Italian administrative practice under occupation law. It is distinct from Cyrenaica and from a sovereign Libyan national government.

governments.value: Lieutenant-governor within the AOF hierarchy; military cercles and local chiefs

governments.value: Government and National Assembly under the 1959 constitution

governments.value: Prime Minister Moktar Ould Daddah and National Assembly

descriptions.value: Spanish Sahara is a colonial framework encompassing Rio de Oro and Sakiet El Hamra. No independent modern Saharan state, geometry-derived local sovereignty or neighboring territorial claim is substituted.

politicalStatus.value: Colonial territory designated a province by Spain

governments.value: Spanish Presidency, African Provinces Directorate and Governor-General

descriptions.value: The 1958 decree created a separate Sahara province under Spanish administration. Domestic provincial naming does not establish international sovereign entitlement or override self-determination. Later 1961 institutions are excluded.

governments.value: Italian colonial military command and local resistance forces

sources.title: Muhammad Ali, 1805–48
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: Ottoman appointment June 1805, consolidation by 1811, hereditary governorship only 1841. Accepted 1815 framework, not retrospective sovereign kingdom.

sources.title: Khedive Ismail, 1863–79
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read body paragraphs 6–8: Khedive title granted by Ottoman sultan, altered succession and increased autonomy, not completed independence.

sources.title: From intervention to occupation, 1876–82
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: European financial controls, 1878 mixed cabinet, Ottoman removal of Ismail 26 June 1879, Tawfiq and renewed dual control; July 1880 Assembly dissolved. Stops before 1881–82 competing authorities.

sources.title: The British occupation
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: Khedive retained; British agent, consul-general and troops held practical power; consultative bodies and 1913 assembly. ERRONEOUS 3 November 1914 protectorate date rejected in favor of primary Hansard 18 December.

sources.title: Situation in Egypt, 15 May 1919
sources.institution: UK Parliament, Hansard
sources.usage: Read ministerial statement body: British protectorate proclaimed 18 December 1914; high commissioner and protectorate constitutional inquiry. This corrects LoC chronology, not proof of British sovereign annexation.

sources.title: Protectorate and 1919 Revolution
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: British high commissioner, nationalist challenges; 28 February 1922 unilateral independence with four reserved British matters. Subsequent April constitution date lacks year here and is not used to date a charter.

sources.title: Liberal constitutionalism and party politics
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read body: King, Wafd and British political triangle; 1930 replacement enhanced monarch powers; 1936 alliance retained British garrison and Sudan control. Stops 1939; no unrestricted independence or democratic-practice claim.

sources.title: Egypt during World War II
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: British pressure on king and cabinet in 1942; Wafd fell 1944, 1945 election brought Liberal Constitutionalists/Saadists. No exact cabinet-change date inferred.

sources.title: Egypt and the Arab World
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: 1958 unitary union with Syria, Nasser presidency and Cairo capital; Syria seceded September 1961. Narrow 1959–1960 avoids guessing union establishment day or applying later Egyptian republic.

sources.title: Historical recognition and relations with Morocco
sources.institution: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.usage: Read historical body: sovereign Sultan treaty 1786, Sultan Suleiman consular gift 1821; protectorate 1912–56, March 1956 independence, Rabat capital. Erroneous simplistic Tangier Spanish-control wording not adopted.

sources.title: Treaty with Morocco, 1786
sources.institution: Yale Law Library, Avalon Project; primary US treaty edition
sources.usage: Read primary royal commission, treaty and articles: Moroccan ruler and government conduct diplomacy. Used with later historical record for early monarchy framework; no named-ruler tenure inferred.

sources.title: Madrid conference and Morocco Convention, 1880
sources.institution: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.usage: Read primary proceedings and convention: Sultan, foreign minister, local governors; sovereign Moroccan authority constrained by consular protections. Narrow 1880 attestation, not 1912 protectorate.

sources.title: US reply concerning Treaty of Fez, 22 January 1913
sources.institution: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.usage: Read primary treaty quotations Articles I and V: Sultan and French government, French Resident sole intermediary abroad. Signed 30 March 1912; partial framework does not imply annexation or equal effective control over all Morocco.

sources.title: French protectorates and mandate archives
sources.institution: French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs
sources.usage: Read archival historical body: Tunisia protectorate 1881–56, Morocco 1912–56 under Foreign Affairs. War regimes/occupation not collapsed into uninterrupted administrative detail.

sources.title: Eisenhower–Mohammed V meeting, 22 December 1959
sources.institution: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.usage: Read primary body: King Mohammed V, Crown Prince, Moroccan government and foreign policy. Used only for independent monarchy core, not US assessments of ideology, economy or control.

sources.title: Rusk memorandum, 17 February 1961
sources.institution: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.usage: Read primary body and notes: King Mohammed V involved in November/December 1960 decisions and February 1961 diplomacy; supports narrow 1960 king framework across adjacent attestations.

sources.title: Administration of the Spanish Protectorate in Morocco
sources.institution: Agencia Estatal Boletin Oficial del Estado, institutional historical collection
sources.usage: Read introduction body: Spanish protectorate 1912–56, Alta Comisaria and administration. Only core 1914 status accepted; detailed Khalifa, institutions and exact zones remain uncurated because full volume fetch failed.

sources.title: Treaty with Tunis, altered 1799 and ratified 1800
sources.institution: Yale Law Library, Avalon Project; primary US treaty edition
sources.usage: Read primary preamble: Ottoman suzerainty invoked, Bey, Dey, Agha and Divan; US ratification January 1800. Only 1800 governmental framework, not full Hamuda tenure.

sources.title: Decatur correspondence, Tunis and Tripoli, 1815
sources.institution: University of North Carolina ibiblio; primary US naval correspondence
sources.usage: Read 25–31 July 1815 correspondence: Bey and Regency of Tunis, prime minister, port authority; August Tripoli Bashaw, governor and prime minister. Source racial/religious and coercive naval judgments excluded.

sources.title: Tunis Residency: correspondence administrative history
sources.institution: French Diplomatic Archives
sources.usage: Read administrative-history body: Resident General directed important French decisions/external relations and was Bey foreign minister after La Marsa. Accepted prewar and postwar narrow frameworks, no named Bey continuity across wartime deposition.

sources.title: Constitution of Tunisia, 1959, original French text
sources.institution: World Intellectual Property Organization, WIPO Lex
sources.usage: Read ORIGINAL FRENCH body Articles 1,18,37–43: independent republic, National Assembly, President executive appoints government. English text on same page is consolidated and excluded. No later Prime Minister or Chamber of Deputies projected into 1960.

sources.title: Historical Constitution of 1959
sources.institution: Ministry of Justice, Tunisia
sources.usage: Read museum historical paragraph: independence 20 March 1956, republic 25 July 1957, constituent assembly and 1959 charter. Later amended constitutional text not used for original institutions.

sources.title: Colonization and military control
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: 1848 three northern departments, separate military areas; 1870 civilian governor-general under Interior; unequal citizenship and exceptional colonial rule. Religious-apostasy simplification excluded; no uniform departmental status across Sahara.

sources.title: Hegemony of the colons
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read historical body: settler-dominated departments, local government and restricted Muslim representation into twentieth century. Source erroneous reference to Algeria National Assembly not copied; relevant body identifies French national representation.

sources.title: Polarization and politicization
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read paragraphs 1–13: Vichy displaced after Allied landings, French governor-general, 1944 limited citizenship reforms, 1945 nationalist protests and violence. Only narrow 1945 colonial government; no 1947 Assembly projected earlier.

sources.title: De Gaulle and Algerian independence war
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read body: French authority, GPRA exile government in Tunis, de Gaulle self-determination announcement 1959 and January 1960 colonial revolt. Source erroneous Fifth Republic and presidential dates excluded. No recognized independent Algeria before 1962.

sources.title: Karamanlis, Tripoli and Ottoman suzerainty
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: hereditary pashalik under nominal Ottoman suzerainty, Yusuf 1795–1832 and extensions to Cyrenaica. Only classification-prerequisite review; region Cyrenaica not automatically separate sovereign polity.

sources.title: Italy and Arab resistance
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: Italian claims contested, 1914 loss of Fezzan, 1917 truce/1920 Idris autonomy and coastal enclaves; 1919 Fundamental Law. Accepted 1914 and 1920 claims frameworks; no all-geometry effective Italian rule.

sources.title: Italian Libya: the Fourth Shore
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: 1934 single colony, four provinces and separate southern military territory; Governor-General and consultative council. Accepted 1935–1938 stops before 1939 coastal annexation; no blanket annexation of Fezzan or whole Libya.

sources.title: Allied administration of Libya
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: separate British Cyrenaica/Tripolitania districts and brigadiers, French Fezzan staff at Sabha through local notables; Ghat and Ghadames command exceptions. Narrow 1945 occupation, not British/French sovereignty.

sources.title: Independent federal Libya
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: 1951 federal monarchy, King, Cabinet, Chamber and Senate, autonomous provinces; parties banned after 1952 election; unitary amendment only April 1963. Accepted narrow 1960 federal framework.

sources.title: French administration through WWII
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: AOF inclusion 1920, lieutenant governor and military cercles, local chiefly administration, no pre1946 legislature. Brazzaville erroneously dated June 1944, not adopted. Narrow 1945 colonial framework only.

sources.title: Independence and civilian rule
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read historical body: autonomous French Community republic, March 1959 charter, National Assembly May 1959 and independence 28 November 1960. Erroneous October 1958 proclamation and later one-party dates not used.

sources.title: Mauritanian independence and US recognition
sources.institution: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.usage: Read historical body: independence recognition 28 November 1960, Prime Minister Daddah, same-day diplomatic credentials. No presidential title projected from later 1961 constitution.

sources.title: Western Sahara Advisory Opinion, 16 October 1975, UN primary-text collection
sources.institution: International Court of Justice; UN Office of Legal Affairs archive
sources.usage: Downloaded scanned PDF; rendered and visually read opinion pages 38–41,44–49,68–69 (PDF indices121–126,136), paragraphs76–88,95–109,162–163. 1884 Rio de Oro protectorate proclamation, organized communities, Spanish colonial administering power; allegiance links did not establish territorial sovereignty. Not the whole 312-page compilation.

sources.title: Decree 10 January 1958, Spanish Sahara administration
sources.institution: Presidency of Government of Spain; primary law reproduced in 1975 document collection
sources.usage: Read primary decree body PDF pages23–24, Articles1–6: separate Sahara province, Presidency through African Provinces Directorate and Governor-General. Later 1961 decree nearby not projected into 1960. Provincial designation described as Spanish domestic colonial administration, not international sovereign entitlement.

sources.title: Second Italo-Sanusi War
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: fascist colonial policy, military reconquest, Umar al-Mukhtar resistance, forced internment and 1931 capture. Unsourced moral psychology, blanket pacification and erroneous barrier chronology not adopted.

limitations: Partial research frameworks for 18 identities; no claim of core or enriched completeness.
Chronological gaps remain explicit, particularly 1878/1900 Morocco, 1930 Egyptian constitutional transition, wartime administrations and detailed colonial offices.
No new leaders arrays or unsupported demographic/financial figures; institutional names within dated government records only.
exclusions: Modern historical fallback; inferred sovereignty/succession; demographic and GDP enrichment; flags; Antarctica; Compare Dates; unrelated UI changes.
Community/people identities not automatically mapped; prerequisite raw regions require separate classification review.
historicalCautions: Egypt protectorate begins 18 December 1914; LoC 3 November chronology rejected using primary Hansard.
1960 Egypt belongs to Egyptian–Syrian United Arab Republic; no modern Egypt republic fallback.
Mauritania independence 28 November 1960 is a within-year transition; prime-minister title retained, 1961 presidency not projected backward.
Tunisia original French 1959 charter used; later consolidated English institutions rejected.
French Algeria northern departments coexist with colonial inequality and military southern administration; 1960 GPRA rival government does not erase French authority.
Libyan colonial claim, effective control and occupation administrations remain distinct; 1939 coastal annexation and 1963 unitary monarchy excluded from accepted earlier frameworks.

Sahara Spanish domestic provincial administration does not establish international sovereignty. ICJ allegiance links do not constitute territorial sovereignty; organized communities are not terra nullius.
Cyrenaica and Tripolitania prerequisites are review-only and do not silently enlarge assignment scope.
